title: Laghman I: An Aramaic inscription associated with Priyadarśin
excerpt: A short Aramaic rock inscription names King Priyadarśin and gives disputed directions and distances. Its status as a royal edict remains uncertain.
html:
About this inscription

Laghman I was found on a rock in Afghanistan. Its first line names King Priyadarśin, and its last names a judge. The intervening words mention measures or distances, a place name, and a road. André Dupont-Sommer read the date as year ten and the place name Tdmr as Tadmor (Palmyra), and translated the opening as a royal moral command. Franz Rosenthal instead read the date as year seventeen and treated the record as a legal verdict. Both the place-name reading and the nature of the text are disputed. Harry Falk likewise cautions that its royal authorship cannot be established. It is included here as an associated inscription, not presented as a certain Ashokan edict.

Original script

The following transcription uses the Aramaic letters in Dupont-Sommer’s edition. The upright strokes separate groups on the stone; the readings of several words remain disputed.

𐡁𐡔𐡍𐡕 𐡛 𐡗 𐡇𐡆𐡉 𐡗 𐡐𐡓𐡉𐡃𐡓𐡔 𐡌𐡋𐡊𐡀 𐡗 𐡓𐡒 𐡃𐡇𐡀
𐡌𐡄 𐡌𐡑𐡃 𐡁𐡓𐡉𐡅𐡕 𐡊𐡅𐡓𐡉
𐡌𐡍 𐡔𐡓𐡉𐡓𐡉𐡍 𐡃𐡅𐡃𐡉 𐡌𐡄 𐡏𐡁𐡃 𐡓𐡉𐡒 𐡒𐡔𐡕𐡍
𐡙 𐡝 𐡆𐡍𐡄 𐡕𐡌𐡄 𐡕𐡃𐡌𐡓 𐡔𐡌𐡄 𐡆𐡍𐡄 𐡀𐡓𐡄𐡀 𐡊𐡍𐡐𐡕𐡉 𐡎𐡄𐡕𐡉
𐡂𐡍𐡕𐡀 𐡉𐡕𐡓𐡉 𐡝 𐡜 𐡕𐡓𐡕𐡀 𐡕𐡍𐡄 𐡝 𐡏𐡋𐡀 𐡜 𐡜 𐡜 𐡜
𐡏𐡌 𐡅𐡀𐡔𐡅 𐡃𐡉𐡍𐡀

Roman transliteration

1. bšnt 10 | ḥzy | Prydrš mlkʾ | rq dḥʾ
2. mh mṣd brywt kwry
3. mn šryryn dwdy mh ʿbd ryq qštn
4. 200 znh rmh Tdmr šmh znh ʾrʾ knpty shty
5. gntʾ ytry 100 20 trtʾ tnh 100 ʿlʾ 20 20 20 20
6. ʿm Wʾšw dynʾ

English translation

All six inscribed lines survive, but their sense is not settled. The rendering below follows Dupont-Sommer’s reading where words can be interpreted and leaves obscure groups untranslated. Rosenthal’s date and legal reading differ substantially.

  1. In year ten [or seventeen in another reading], [the inscription] names King Priyadarśin. The rest of the line is uncertain. 2–3. Words read as a statement about vanity, friends, and fishing; the syntax and meaning are disputed.
  2. A distance of 200 [units] is given, followed by a place written Tdmr and a road name. Whether Tdmr refers to Palmyra is disputed.
  3. Further numbers and distances are recorded; their units and destinations are uncertain.
  4. The final line names Wʾšw, a judge.

Sources

  • André Dupont-Sommer, “Une nouvelle inscription araméenne d’Asoka trouvée dans la vallée du Laghman” (1970), Comptes rendus des séances de l’Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres 114(1), pp. 158–173 (text, image, and interpretation).
  • Harry Falk, Aśokan Sites and Artefacts (2006), pp. 259–262 (alternative reading and attribution caution).
  • Image record, Wikimedia Commons.
